1:
Whether this continues the previous quarrel or begins a new occasion is disputed. Barnes argues from the formula, since the doubled asseveration is not used to open a discourse, so that this follows straight on from the charge of blindness laid against men claiming to be shepherds. Henry leaves it open, noting that the later mention of the winter feast may date what precedes as well as what follows, the sheep metaphor being still in use when that feast is named. Clarke reports both datings, one putting the discourse immediately after the last, the other three months later.

Ellicott raises a question of method before the details are pressed. The word used is not the ordinary word for parable, which this evangelist never uses, but a wider one covering any figurative speech; and the difference is not merely verbal, since in a parable the outer story is kept distinct from the truth it carries, while here form and idea interpenetrate at every point. He concludes that neither this discourse nor the vine is strictly a parable, and that every particular, the porter expressly, is not to be pressed.

The particulars are pressed nonetheless, and the porter is the test case. Chrysostom suggests Moses, as the man to whom the oracles of God were committed. Augustine offers the Lord himself, since there is far less distance between a door and a porter than between a door and a shepherd, and he has already called himself both; if another person is wanted, take the Spirit who guides into all truth, but never esteem the porter greater than the door. On the door itself Chrysostom makes it the Scriptures, which admit us to the knowledge of God and bar the entrance to heretics, so that climbing another way means a self-chosen path, or the traditions of men taught to the neglect of the Law; and the verb is not entering but climbing, like a thief going over a wall. He resolves the shifting figure by office: bringing us to the Father he is the door, caring for us the shepherd.

Augustine turns the same verse against respectable unbelief. Many pass for good men by the world's measure and keep the Law after a fashion without being Christians; but a good life profits only as it leads to life eternal, and those cannot be said to live well who despise its end. He adds the image the others lack: Christ is a lowly door, and whoever would come through with his head whole must stoop. Barnes applies it narrowly to the ministry, the Pharisees having claimed the pastoral office without the appointment that alone opens it, and observes that in every church many have sought that office from ambition or love of ease.

Lightfoot alone describes the thing itself. The fold was a pen where the flock was gathered at night and milked by day, and where the lambs were tithed: the flock driven in, a little door made at which two could not pass together, the lambs counted out and the tenth marked with red, the ewes left outside so that the lambs came out at their bleating. So there were two doors, a larger for the flock, a smaller for tithing. He also supplies the legal distinction the terms carry, a thief taking when the owner is not privy and a robber openly and by force, the same line Barnes draws between stealth and bloodshed.

Two smaller disagreements remain. Chrysostom says shepherds always go behind their flocks and this one goes before, which is the point; Henry says going before was the custom of the country, the shepherd walking ahead to meet danger. And Augustine will not tidy away a difficulty: sometimes those who are not sheep hear the voice, since the traitor heard it, and sometimes the sheep do not, since some who crucified him were his sheep.
7:
The sweeping clause about all who came before is the crux of the passage, and nobody will take it at face value. Chrysostom denies flatly that the prophets are meant, as he says the heretics take it, and names instead the agitators who had lately troubled the nation; he supports the reading from the next clause, since the sheep are praised for not hearing these men, whereas those who disobeyed the prophets are everywhere condemned. Gill works through the exceptions: not Moses, not the prophets of the Lord, not the Baptist who prepared the way, but those who came unsent, and the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. He adds a particular identification, the three shepherds cut off in one month, which he takes for the three sects and their leaders.

Lightfoot takes up the same identification and then makes a historical argument the others do not. He would gladly have referred the words to men who had claimed the title of Messiah and imposed themselves on the people, except that he can find hardly a single instance of anyone doing so before the true Messiah came, whereas after that coming there were a great many. He treats the asymmetry as evidence, that the moment when Jesus appeared was precisely the moment the nation was looking for the Messiah. Barnes reaches the same conclusion independently, that there is no evidence of any pretended Messiah before him, and settles on the scribes and Pharisees as the men meant; he also disarms the word all, which is used here in the popular sense the New Testament often gives it, for the great mass rather than every individual.

On the door itself Ellicott sets the saying beside the strait gate and the narrow way, and draws the line firmly in both directions: no shepherd enters the fold except through the character and life and death of Christ, and we may not narrow that door, nor yet may we widen it.

What going in and out means is answered three ways. Chrysostom refers it to the apostles, who went in and out boldly and became the masters of the world, so that nobody could turn them out of their kingdom. Clarke takes it as a Hebrew idiom covering the whole activity of a life and the liberty of acting or not acting, and applies it to the shepherd who leads the flock to good pasture, watches there, and brings them back to the fold. Ellicott keeps the freedom rather than the range: the fold stands always open to the man who came in by the door, so that he may enter whenever storm or night approaches, and go out again to find food for others. Lightfoot supplies a drier note from the rabbis, who fixed the distance a beast might go out to pasture at sixteen miles, which he calls a spacious pasture indeed.

The last clause is read as a promise of more than survival. Barnes distinguishes bare existence from the abundance superadded to it, arguing that it would be great mercy merely to keep men from destruction, and that what is offered instead is peace, the society of the blessed, and the means of happiness prepared in glory. Clarke measures the same abundance historically, as blessings greater than were ever enjoyed under the older dispensation, even in the promised land. Gill turns to the thief on the other side of the contrast, whose aim is to carry the sheep away from their shepherd and steal their hearts as a rebel prince once stole the hearts of a kingdom from his father. Clarke is fiercer: men who enter the ministry for its revenues are the basest of thieves, their doctrine deadly because it comes from no commission; and he adds that the charge is not to be applied to any one class of preachers only.
11:
Augustine takes up the difficulty the two images make together. If he is the door, how does he enter by himself? The answer is drawn from another relation: as he knows the Father by himself and we by him, so he enters the fold by himself and we by him; we come in by the door because we preach Christ, while Christ preaches himself, a light showing both other things and itself. From this he draws the limit on the office. There is one Shepherd, and the rulers of the Church who are sons and not hirelings are shepherds only as members of him; Peter is a shepherd and so are all good bishops, but none of us calls himself the door. He adds the observation the adjective forces: good could not have been added unless there were bad shepherds too.

Who the hireling is gets answered carefully. Ellicott rules out the obvious target, the hierarchy having already been called thieves and robbers, and takes the word for anyone who enters the office from a motive other than love of men, or by any door but Christ; the Greek, he notes, implies something below a household servant. Barnes describes the type concretely: a minister who preaches for support, will run no risk, and would rather see the church wasted by its enemies than lose his reputation or place. Clarke's old English Bible gave him the word merchant, of one who makes merchandise of men's souls, and he sets the two figures against each other exactly: the hireling counts the sheep his own only so long as they are profitable to him, and the good shepherd counts them his own so long as he can be profitable to them. He adds a caution the others do not, that no reader should fasten this on one class of men, since every party may have its hireling, and the danger is greatest where the provision is largest.

Augustine locates the fault deeper than the wages. Such a man seeks in the Church not God but something else; had he sought God he would be chaste, the soul having one lawful husband, and whoever seeks from God anything besides God seeks unchastely.

He also refuses to let suffering settle the question. Those who laid down their lives were good shepherds not because they shed their blood but because they shed it for the sheep, in love and not in pride; men troubled by the consequences of their own errors will claim a martyrdom at once, and steal under so fair a cloak, being wolves; and not everyone who gives his body to be burned sheds blood for the sheep, some shedding it against them, since such a gift without charity profits nothing.

The knowing is read as loving rather than as information. Barnes says the word carries affectionate regard, and points out that the knowledge of this verse is glossed by love a few verses later. Clarke agrees and adds a parallel from Homer, goatherds separating their own beasts with ease though the flocks feed mixed together. Ellicott objects that the verse division obscures the sentence, which should run on so that the mutual knowledge of Father and Son is not a separate assertion but the measure of the union between shepherd and sheep. Robertson keeps the proportion honest: no one may claim a knowledge like that between Father and Son, and yet the sheep really do know the voice and follow it in spite of thieves and hirelings. Calvin declines the speculative question, how the Father knows his own Wisdom, and holds to what is said: Christ stands between God and us as the bond of the union, so that it is no more possible for him to forget us than for the Father to disregard him. Chrysostom adds only what the last clause secures, that the passion was not undergone unwillingly.
16:
The present tense in I have other sheep is where the weight falls. Barnes refuses to let it mean that these were already friends, and takes it instead for a purpose so settled that it could be spoken of as accomplished, comparing the assurance given at Corinth that God had much people in that city. He then presses the inference hard: the certainty cannot rest on any disposition foreseen in them, since they were the most corrupt people of antiquity, so it must rest on the intention of God; from which he draws that salvation is no matter of chance, and that a preacher has ground to expect success. Gill reads the clause the same way, of the elect among the Gentiles, sheep before they are called or folded, given to Christ and already in his hands.

On the one fold Barnes keeps the historical edge, that this was a plain intimation of a gospel for the Gentiles, a doctrine extremely offensive to those hearing it, and that the partition was to come down so completely that no national privilege or pre-eminence of rank would remain.

Why the Father's love is grounded on the laying down of the life troubles Ellicott, who calls the verse difficult and does not pretend otherwise. His reading is that the reason of the love lies in the self-devotion of the Son, so that he who gave his Son for the world loves the Son who of his own will gives himself; it is almost as though the salvation of mankind had called out a new relation of love between them. He adds what most readers pass over, that the taking of the life again is given as part of the reason of that love, and that the words admit no other construction, though at first sight this runs against common feeling about sacrifice. Gill spreads the love wider, over the Son as Son from eternity, as Mediator, as clothed with our nature and as suffering in our room, and states the hard half plainly, that the bruising was a pleasure to the Father not in itself but because by it the counsel was accomplished.

Clarke hears the clause as an answer to something the hearers were about to think. They were not to imagine, when they saw him crucified, that he had been abandoned by his Father and so fallen into their hands; nor that he was put to death because he lacked the strength to resist. The Father loves him on this very account, that he is going to lay down his life for the life of the world.

That the death was voluntary is then argued from the record rather than asserted. Gill grants everything the history says, that the rulers procured it and the soldiers carried it out and that his life was taken from the earth, and still holds that none of them could have taken it without the Father's will and his own consent, since he went freely to the cross and could have come down from it. Barnes argues from the escapes, that a man who had so often slipped through his enemies' hands and who went up to Jerusalem knowing what waited there was not overtaken; and he defends the right to do it by ordinary cases, the patriot who dies on the field and the merchant who risks his life for gain, so that the Son of God might put himself in the way of death when a dying world needed the sacrifice. Origen reaches the same point from the other end, taking the lamb led to the slaughter and the lamb standing as if slain, and finding in this very saying the proof that the one who led that lamb to the slaughter was God in man, the great High Priest.
19:
Henry takes the division as the expected result rather than an accident. The sayings ought to have gathered them round a common centre and instead set them at odds, which is what had been foretold; and he notes drily that a congregation once split is not easily mended, rents being sooner made than made up. He will not treat the split as simply bad, since it is better that men should be divided about the doctrine of Christ than united in the service of sin. Barnes says the same about preaching in general, that this teaching always produced an effect and made either bitter enemies or decided friends, as all faithful preaching will, so that the divisions are to be laid at the door of unbelief and not of the gospel.

What the accusation actually charged is disputed. Clarke insists that a demoniac and a madman were not the same thing to that people, and that the two terms are here distinguished rather than repeated: they held him possessed by a spirit which deranged his faculties, and inferred that he must have been a wicked man to be given over to such a spirit at all. Ellicott takes the second clause for an explanation of the first, the madness being simply what possession looks like. Gill supplies the background both are working from, the Jewish notion of a particular evil spirit that takes away a man's understanding. Robertson is brusque about the motive: it was an easy way of discounting him, and had been used before.

Henry hears two charges in the sentence and not one. The first falls on the speaker, and he observes that the worst of characters is regularly fastened on the best of men, so that anyone who preaches in earnest about another world will be called an enthusiast and his conduct put down to a heated brain. The second falls on the audience, in the question why they listen at all; and here he is sharpest, that men are ruined by being laughed out of their regard for the word, though they would never allow themselves to be laughed out of their food, which is less necessary. Calvin reads the tactic the same way: the reproach is the most offensive one they can devise, chosen so that everybody may shudder at the thought of hearing him, and raised loudly enough that not a single word should be heard in silence; but he adds that the doctrine has power enough in itself to answer such slanders.

On the defenders the commentators are warmer than the text requires. Henry notices what it cost them, since the stream ran strong and they swam against it, and suspects that they did not believe him to be the Christ and simply could not bear to hear him abused; unreasonable attacks often bringing men to a defence they would not otherwise undertake. Gill counts the numbers the other way about, the accusers many and the better sort few. Ellicott identifies the speakers as the same moderate party in the council that had appeared once before.

Clarke takes their argument seriously and completes it. The words themselves are words of sense and sobriety, which is not how possession sounds; and beyond the words there is the fact that this man had opened the eyes of one born blind, which no demon does. From that he turns to the bearing of the accused, that not a word of impatience escaped him under such usage, and asks what he had done to deserve it: he was instructing the ignorant and telling the wretched that he was about to die for them. He draws the practical conclusion for ministers, that a disciple should not expect better treatment than his master, and notes that on this occasion the friendly voices carried the day and the others left the field.
22:
Which dedication is meant is not agreed. Chrysostom takes it for the dedication of the temple after the return from Babylon. Everyone else takes it for the feast of the Maccabees, and Barnes and Clarke tell the story: the city taken, forty thousand killed and as many sold, a sow sacrificed on the altar and broth from it sprinkled through the house, the service suspended three years, then the purifying with eight days of hymns and gold crowns set on the front of the temple. Augustine supplies only the word, that any dedication of a new thing was called by the Greek name for new. Robertson notes that the term occurs nowhere else in the New Testament.

Henry makes a distinction about the kind of day it was. The celebration was not confined to Jerusalem, as the divinely appointed feasts were, but kept by every man in his own place, and kept not as a holy time, since only a divine institution can sanctify a day, but as a good time, like the days of Purim. Robertson says the same in fewer words, that this was not one of the great feasts and could be observed anywhere. Henry adds that Christ came up not in honour of a feast that did not require his attendance, but to use the eight days of vacation.

The note about winter is read as weather rather than calendar. Clarke argues that there was no need to tell a reader it was winter when everyone knew the date, so the word likelier means stormy or rainy, which explains the walking under cover. Barnes takes it the same way, as cold and inclement and given expressly as the reason for the portico. Augustine lets the season stand as a figure, the men who came being cold in love and burning in malevolence, and approaching not to honour but to persecute.

The gap before this scene interests the harmonisers. Clarke observes that the evangelist passes over everything between the autumn feast and this one, probably because the others had covered it, and counts this the fourth of the four visits to Jerusalem that this Gospel alone records. Ellicott puts the interval at about two months, cites a calculation dating the one feast to mid-October and this to the twentieth of December, and fills the gap from the third Gospel. Robertson allows nearly three months and refuses a proposed rearrangement of the chapter as purely arbitrary.

Lightfoot is the only one who looks hard at the feast's other name. It was called the feast of Lights, and he will not accept the explanation offered for it: one would suppose from the name that candles were lit, and there is no mention of any; one would also suppose the eight days copied from Tabernacles, and the rabbinic authorities say otherwise, in what he calls a cunning way of talking about it. Henry and Barnes agree about the porch itself, which took Solomon's name not from being built by him but from standing where his porch had stood in the first temple, the name kept up for the credit of the place; Henry adds that the council sat there.

On the question put to him the two fathers agree. Chrysostom finds the perversity in the pattern: when he teaches by discourse they demand a sign, and when he demonstrates by works they demand a plain word, being determined to oppose either way. He hears malice in the phrase itself, since nothing had been hidden at the feasts, and takes the courteous preface for flattery meant to draw out something they could use. Augustine says what they were angling for, a bare confession that he was the Christ, which men holding merely human notions of the Messiah could then turn into a charge of aspiring to a throne.
25:
The promise of the flock's safety is read as strongly as the words allow. Barnes presses the original, which he renders as a declaration that they shall not be destroyed for ever, and cites a version that has them not perishing to eternity; the verb for plucking, he adds, means to rob, to seize and carry off as a robber does his prey, so that the picture is of an attempted theft that cannot succeed. The word any he takes to cover every power that might attempt it, man or devil, eloquent in error or mighty in rank, and none of them able. Gill reads the gift in the same direction, that the life given is already begun in a life of grace, held for them in their representative, and spoken of as given now because it is certain.

Ellicott notices the shape of the argument rather than its force. The thought mounts with each succeeding sentence: first that none shall pluck them out of the Son's hand, then that they were the Father's gift and the Father is greater than all, then that none shall pluck them out of the Father's hand. On that word all he refuses any limiting addition, since it reaches to every creature and every power, and, as he adds carefully, even to the Son considered in his subordination to the Father. Robertson stays with the manuscripts, where the readings differ between a masculine and a neuter both in the relative and in the comparative, and judges the neuter the likelier.

Barnes draws the doctrine out in order and does not soften it: that the people are given by the Father to the Son, that the Son gives them the life which issues in glory, that Father and Son are alike pledged to keep them, and that no power in man or devil can defeat it. He states plainly that no language could teach the perseverance of the saints more explicitly. He then turns it into a test rather than a comfort, since the only evidence anyone has of belonging to that flock is the persevering resignation of himself to God day after day; a man who does that is safe, and a man who does not has no evidence of piety and is not safe.

Clarke keeps to the one clause about the Father's greatness, which he glosses as more powerful than all the united energies of men and demons, and draws from it the plainest of consequences: whoever loves God must be happy, and whoever fears him need fear nothing on this side of eternity.

The closing sentence is the disputed one, and Barnes sets out the case at length. He begins by conceding what the grammar will not give him, since the word for one is neuter and expresses union without specifying its kind, and he reports that able interpreters have taken it of a union of design and counsel only. His own argument for a union of nature runs in four steps: the point in debate was power and not counsel, since the claim was to keep the flock against all creation; the hearers plainly understood a claim of equality, because they took up stones and said so; the speaker did not deny that this was his meaning; and he immediately said something else that produced the same effect. To these he adds a moral consideration, that if he had not intended to be so understood, his failure to disavow it can hardly be reconciled with honesty. Gill reaches the same conclusion by the grammar the others pass over, that the verb is plural, so that the sentence cannot mean one person but must mean one in nature and essence, and here particularly one in power, since the whole point at issue is whether the same hand holds the sheep.
31:
The argument from the reaction is made by three writers who had no chance of borrowing it from each other. Augustine puts it most sharply, that the men who took up stones understood what a later party of interpreters did not; they were angry precisely because they could not take the words about being one with the Father as meaning anything short of equality. Chrysostom makes the same point from the reply rather than the offence: the speaker did not correct them as men who had misheard him, but confirmed and defended what he had said in the very sense they had taken it. Clarke reaches the conclusion by a test of his own. Had they understood no more than a unity of sentiment with the Father, they would not have treated it as blasphemy at all, since in that sense Abraham and Moses and every prophet was one with God; what enraged them was that they heard a unity of nature, which is how the word God in their answer is to be read, in its literal meaning and not in a figure.

What the good works were is described without disagreement but not without emphasis. Gill lists them as works of power that were also works of mercy, the sick healed, the possessed delivered, the lepers cleansed, the blind given sight. Barnes notes that these were the only works there were to appeal to, so that the appeal could be made confidently, and adds the reflection that it would be a happy thing if everyone under persecution could point his persecutors to such a record of his own innocence. Clarke explains the idiom, since to show good works in that language means to do them in earnest and give good things liberally, and he supports it from several psalms where showing mercy or showing hard things means simply dealing so.

Ellicott dissents about which quality of the works is in view. The word does not make their beneficence prominent, he argues, but their moral excellence, and no English word quite carries it, though excellent or distinguished come nearer than good; and these are works from the Father made visible in the world by the Son. He notices too that the question uses a word marking quality rather than mere distinction, so that it asks what kind of work deserves stoning; and in the reply the preposition is not the causal one of the previous verse but the word proper to an indictment, so that the sentence has the form of a charge laid.

Robertson reads the same reply as a piece of evasion. Taken literally it denies that any good deed had brought them to this, which flatly contradicts what had happened after the healing on the sabbath; and he observes that the charge had been stated more accurately on an earlier occasion, where the offence was calling God his own Father and so making himself equal with God. He grants the fact at once, that this is what the speaker did, and then puts the only question that matters: it was blasphemy only if he was not the Son of God. He adds what hung on the answer, since the penalty for blasphemy was death by stoning.

Two smaller notes complete the scene. Clarke distinguishes the two uses of the word for blasphemy, which applied to men means speaking injuriously of a person or character, and applied to God means speaking impiously, contrary to his nature and perfections and the wisdom of his providence. Calvin observes the constant habit behind the indictment, that wicked men carry on open war with God and still will not sin without first finding some plausible cover for it.
34:
That the word law here covers more than the books of Moses is agreed, since the sentence quoted comes from a psalm; Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott all note the wider usage. On whom the psalm calls gods they also agree. Barnes takes it of magistrates, named so for the dignity of the office, and remarks that such a use of the word is rare. Clarke says the same of judges and thinks this probably the only place in the Hebrew where the word is applied to any but the true God. Ellicott adds that the pronoun is emphatic in both Hebrew and Greek, so that the sentence runs I myself said ye are gods, and reads the psalm as God sitting in judgment on the judges he had appointed and giving them a name that represents himself.

Lightfoot reports what the rabbis had made of the same verse and does not conceal his opinion of it. They took it to mean that had the fathers not sinned with the calf their children would never have been born, since they would have been like angels and begotten none, and that the law was given only so that death should not rule over them. He calls this a most ridiculous sense, and sets against it a reading he thinks the whole contexture of the psalm requires, that it speaks of the magistracy, to whom the word of God came as an express commission and warrant for governing.

What the argument proves is stated with unusual care by Barnes, who is careful also about what it does not. The clause that Scripture cannot be broken settles the authority of the text: if the word god is there applied to men in office, its application to men is not in itself blasphemous. But he then lists what the speaker declined to do. He did not deny that he meant the term of himself; he did not deny that it was properly applied to him; he did not deny that it implied he was God. What he affirmed was narrower, that his accusers were inconsistent, and had no warrant for a charge of blasphemy founded on a word their own Scriptures use of magistrates.

The word sanctified is read three ways. Barnes insists it cannot mean made holy, since the Son was always holy, and takes it for setting apart from a common to a sacred use, the consecration of a man to an office. Gill puts the act far earlier, in the eternal separation of the Son to the work of Mediator before the foundation of the world, and argues that this presupposes his eternal existence and so proves his deity by implication. Ellicott fixes the tense on a moment instead, the consecration to the Messianic work and the Incarnation which began it.

On the appeal to the works the commentators divide by temper rather than doctrine. Clarke calls the reasoning conclusive: the only way to weaken it was to deny that the miracles were wrought by the power of God, which would have obliged the accusers to maintain that a bad man could work them, so that the argument had a complete triumph. Ellicott is gentler and more exacting at once. A higher faith would have believed the speaker himself, and had they known their own need they would have found in him what the mind craves; failing that, he takes their lower ground and appeals to what can be seen, preferring a reading which asks them to perceive first and then to know permanently, so that perception of the character of the works becomes the step up to knowing that such works can only be the Father's. Barnes says only that none could do them unless sent from God, and that the phrase about the Father being in him denotes a union possible in no other case.
39:
Bede marks the persistence rather than the escape, that they were still in the same madness and tried once more to seize him. Gill draws a distinction in the attempt, that this was not the furious stoning of a moment earlier but a design to lay hold of him and bring him before the council, which is a different and colder intention. Barnes turns the retreat into a general observation, that the persecution was itself the occasion of the journey, so that the wrath of men was made to serve the cause they opposed, as it has commonly happened that opposition has ended in the increased success of what it attacked.

Where he went is a geographical puzzle and the commentators disagree about it. Clarke denies that the phrase means the far bank at all and would render it to the side of Jordan rather than beyond it. Ellicott takes the opposite view and works the problem out at length, noting that the province proper lay west of the river and that an old tribal boundary explains how the name spread eastward, and settling on a place north of the lake on the eastern side. Lightfoot answers a different question, identifying the spot by the earlier narrative as the Bethabara where the baptising began, and Barnes agrees with him.

Ellicott reads the withdrawal as a turning point. The teaching had been by divine words and they took up stones; the appeal had been to divine works and they tried to take him by force; and in both he sees the darkness that comes before night, so that the retirement from the city is a leaving of it unvisited until the last Passover. He sets the lament over Jerusalem beside it. Yet he refuses to let the chapter end in the dark, since it is one of the notes struck in the opening words of this Gospel and sounded at intervals ever since that the light is never wholly absent; against the rejection at the capital he sets the reception on the old ground, where the memories were early ones and the hopes were now being answered.

What the people said about the Baptist is examined more closely than it looks. Barnes points out the form of their reasoning, that John gave no miracle but foretold the character and the success of the one who came after, and that either a miracle or a prophecy is conclusive proof of a mission, since no man can do either without God. He adds that the ministry in that place had prepared them for what followed. Ellicott makes the same absence a kind of evidence: the Baptist did no sign and so fell short of the glory of the one whose signs they had now seen, and yet he had recognised that glory further than anyone else of his generation, so that his insight was itself a sign, and everything he had said was verified by what had since happened.

Clarke puts the two grounds of their belief in order, the testimony of a man they knew to be honest and a prophet, and the miracles they had seen for themselves, which together proved that what he had said was true. Then he draws a comparison: the scribes and Pharisees with all their learning could not reach a conclusion so plain, and truth and common sense are often found with ordinary people, whom the insolently wise and the tyrannically powerful are willing enough to dismiss as a mob. He ends by setting this chapter beside the last as two defeats of the same doctors, the first administered by an uneducated man who did nothing but appeal to a matter of fact, the second by a wisdom from above; and he concludes that God sometimes silences gainsayers himself, and sometimes makes the simplest of his followers too strong for the most learned.
